I hear how much weight is behind this question — it's not just philosophical for you, it's raw. And I want to be honest: I don't think there's an answer that makes a child's suffering feel okay. Anyone who tries to hand you a tidy explanation that erases the horror of it is dodging something real. So let me try to share what these sources actually say, without pretending it resolves the pain.

**Freedom and its cost.** EveryStudent puts it starkly: humans are "pretty much free to do as we choose," and God "does not interfere with anyone's choices." The suggestion is that a world where love and moral choice are real requires a world where cruelty is also genuinely possible — God could have made a world of puppets who can't hurt each other, but that's not the kind of freedom or relationship he seems to have built us for ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/why-do-we-worship-god.html)).

**This isn't the whole story, and suffering isn't the "final word."** Cru's piece frames it this way: "The Bible shows us very clearly that God is good and ultimately does not want people to suffer, but that suffering is nevertheless a reality in this life." It points to a larger arc — how suffering entered the world, and God's plan to end it — rather than suffering being evidence God doesn't care ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/life-and-relationships/hardships/why-does-god-allow-suffering.html)).

**Some suffering is just built into a physical world.** One source (Sightline Ministry) points to the story of the man born blind — Jesus was asked whose sin caused it, and he said neither. Some suffering comes from others' choices, some from a physical world governed by consistent laws (gravity, disease, accidents) that God doesn't selectively suspend even for the innocent: "God doesn't take those laws away for good people" ([Sightline Ministry](https://sightlineministry.org/daily-devo/hey-i-dont-deserve-this)).

**And here's the part I think matters most for your question**: thelife.com argues that Christianity's answer isn't primarily an argument — it's that God didn't stay distant from this. "He has given us a clue... that he does have good reasons for allowing evil... He showed us that we could trust him by appearing in human form. And what did he do when he was here? HE SUFFERED!" The claim is that Jesus entered into suffering rather than explaining it away from a safe distance — and that "a child who is hurting needs not an intellectual explanation, but reassurance" ([thelife](https://thelife.com/do-evil-and-suffering-disprove-the-existence-of-god-part-3)).

I want to be straight with you: none of this is a logical proof that closes the case. It's more like — God's response to the problem of suffering isn't an argument, it's a person who suffered too. Whether that lands as comfort or as still not enough is something only you can weigh. Can I ask — is this question coming from something happening around you right now, or more from watching the world and struggling with it?

That's a really good question to ask — and it's not a sign that something's wrong with you for finding it puzzling. Christians themselves acknowledge it's genuinely mysterious.

Here's the key move that resolves the *apparent* contradiction: God is one in **essence**, but three in **person**. According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity," these are two different categories, not the same claim twice. It would only be a contradiction if Christians said God is three in the *same way* he is one (source: [Cru, "Entender la Trinidad"](https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).

So concretely, the doctrine holds three things together:
1. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are **distinct persons** — not just three names or three roles for the same individual. Cru's article points out that since "the Father sent the Son into the world" (John 3:16) and the Father and Son together "sent the Holy Spirit into the world" (John 14:26; Acts 2:33), they can't simply be the same person wearing different masks (source: [Cru, "Understanding the Trinity: A Christian Core Belief"](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).
2. Each person — Father, Son, and Spirit — is **fully God**. The Bible calls the Father God, calls Jesus God, and calls the Holy Spirit God (same Cru source).
3. Yet there is **only one God**, one essence, one "being" — not three beings or three gods.

EveryStudent.com puts it with a memorable bit of math: it's not 1+1+1=3, but more like 1×1×1=1. "Tri" (three) + "unity" (one) = Trinity — God is three Persons sharing one essence of deity (source: [EveryStudent, "Can You Explain the Trinity?"](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).

People have reached for analogies to make this less abstract — water existing as liquid, ice, and steam while remaining H2O, or the sun giving off light, heat, and radiation as three distinct effects of one sun (sources: [EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html) and the German EveryStudent site, [Dreieinigkeit](https://www.duentscheidest.com/artikel/dreieinigkeit.html)). But it's worth being honest: every one of these analogies is admitted to fall short, because there's nothing else in creation that is both fully unified and fully personal in three distinct ways at once. As Cru's "Is Jesus God or Just a Good Man?" article puts it, "all human explanations fall short. Humans are limited in their understanding."

So the short answer to "isn't this a contradiction?" — no, because "one" and "three" are answering different questions (essence vs. person), not the same question twice. But it remains a *mystery* in the proper sense: not irrational, but beyond full human comprehension.

What's prompting the question for you — is it more the logical puzzle, or are you wondering what difference it actually makes for how Christians relate to God?

That's a great and important question—one that comes up often in conversations between Christians and Muslims, since both faiths honor Jesus but understand him very differently.

**What Christians affirm:**

Christians agree that Jesus is a prophet—but say he is *more* than a prophet. As **Cru** puts it: "Muslims believe Jesus to be a prophet but not God in the flesh, whereas Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the Son of God" (Cru, "What Makes Christianity Different?" — https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html). This is a genuine and significant difference, not a minor one—it shapes how each faith understands salvation, the crucifixion, and the resurrection. Muslims don't believe Jesus was crucified or rose from the dead, while Christians hold these as "fundamental truths" of their faith (Cru, same source).

**On the "Son of God" language:**

This phrase can sound troubling from an Islamic perspective, since Islam strongly guards the oneness of God (tawhid) and rejects any idea that God would have a literal, physical son. **EveryStudent.sk** addresses this directly: Christianity does not understand Jesus's sonship "in a bodily sense, but in a spiritual sense. Jesus is God incarnate, who was not born from a physical union of man and woman, but through the miraculous work of the Holy Spirit" (EveryStudent.sk, "Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely" — https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame). Christians point to the prophet Isaiah, who long before Jesus's birth foretold: "For to us a child is born, to us a son is given... and his name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (as cited in EveryStudent.sk, same source).

**On why Jesus would be more than a prophet:**

**EveryStudent.com**'s article "Jesus in Islam" frames it this way: Christians see Jesus not as one prophet among many replacing an earlier revelation, but as the fulfillment of what God had been promising all along through Abraham, Moses, and the prophets (EveryStudent.com, "Jesus in Islam" — https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html). Jesus himself said, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me," as quoted in **EveryStudent.sk** (https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)—a claim that goes beyond what a prophet typically claims for himself.

**A personal note:**

One story worth mentioning: **EveryStudent.com** shares the testimony of a man raised in a strict Muslim household who found himself unexpectedly drawn to Jesus while reading the Quran and Hadiths, eventually asking a Christian friend for a Bible—at real personal risk (EveryStudent.com, "What a radical Muslim came to realize about God." — https://www.everystudent.com/wires/radical.html). It shows that this isn't just an abstract theological debate—it's something people wrestle with deeply and personally.

If you're exploring this question yourself—whether from a Muslim background or just curious—I'm glad to keep digging into any part of it with you. Is there a particular angle you'd like to explore further, like the crucifixion, the resurrection, or what "Son of God" means to Christians?

That's a really honest and fair question to ask — and it's worth digging into carefully.

**The short answer: Jesus never says the exact English phrase "I am God."** But according to the sources I found, he made several statements that his listeners understood as claims to divinity — and those claims are recorded as his own direct words, not just later theological commentary.

Here are the clearest examples, drawn from **Sightline Ministry** (https://sightlineministry.org/jesus-say-he-is-god and https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false) and **Jesus Film Project** (https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/jesus-facts):

1. **"Before Abraham was born, I am!"** (John 8:58) — Jesus uses the same phrase God used to identify himself to Moses at the burning bush ("I AM," Exodus 3:14). According to Jesus Film Project, the crowd's reaction shows they understood this as a divine claim — they picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy.

2. **"I and the Father are one."** (John 10:30) — Sightline Ministry notes that a respected Greek scholar, A.T. Robertson, explains the Greek word "one" here points to unity in essence or nature, not just purpose. The Jewish leaders again responded by trying to stone him.

3. At his trial, the high priest asked Jesus directly, **"Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?"** Jesus answered, **"I am."** (Mark 14:61–62, as cited by Sightline Ministry). The high priest tore his robes and cried "Blasphemy!" — a reaction that only makes sense if Jesus's answer was understood as a claim to divine identity.

4. **"My Father is always working, and so am I."** (John 5:17) — Sightline Ministry points out that by saying "MY Father" rather than "our Father," Jesus was placing himself on equal footing with God in a way his Jewish audience couldn't misread — and John 5:18 records that this is exactly how they took it, wanting to kill him "because he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God."

So while Jesus doesn't use the literal sentence "I am God," his actual recorded words — especially "I am" (echoing God's name) and "I and the Father are one" — were taken by the people standing right there as unmistakable divine claims. That's not later interpretation layered on; it's how his own contemporaries reacted in the moment, according to these texts.

If you want, I can dig further into any one of these passages — like the context around John 8:58 or the trial scene in Mark — to see the fuller conversation around them.

That's a really common concern, and it's good that you're asking rather than just taking it at face value. The short answer, based on the sources I found: your uncle's concern makes sense on the surface, but scholars actually have strong tools to address it — and the evidence points the other way.

**Here's the key issue:** We don't have the *original* handwritten manuscripts of any biblical book — that's true of basically all ancient literature. But that doesn't mean we're lost. As Sightline Ministry explains, "we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts... there are enough existing manuscripts that we can compare and cross-check them to reconstruct what the originals would have said. With proper technique, we can do this with a very high degree of accuracy" (Sightline Ministry, "Has the Bible Been Altered Over the Centuries?", https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries).

**The numbers matter here.** According to EveryStudent ("Jesus in Islam," https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html), there are nearly 25,000 hand-written copies of portions of the New Testament, and when historians compare them, "the New Testament we have today is at least 99.5% accurate to the original" — with most of that remaining 0.5% being things like spelling variations, not changes in meaning. That same source notes complete Bibles exist dating back to 300 A.D., and comparing those to today's Bible shows they're essentially the same.

**Compared to other ancient texts, the Bible is unusually well-attested.** The Spanish EveryStudent source (cadaestudiante.com, "Libros de la Biblia - Historia de la Biblia") gives a helpful comparison: works like Plato's writings or Herodotus's Histories survive in only 5–20 copies, with gaps of 1,000+ years between the original and the oldest surviving copy. The New Testament has vastly more manuscripts and much smaller time gaps — which is exactly what scholars use to cross-check and reconstruct the original wording with confidence.

**On translation specifically**, the Vietnamese EveryStudent source makes an important clarification: translations aren't a game of "telephone" where each translation is based on the previous translation. Modern translations go back directly to the original Greek, Hebrew, and Aramaic manuscripts (EveryVietStudent.com, "Các sách của Kinh Thánh - Lịch sử của Kinh Thánh").

So it's fair to say scribes made some copying errors over the centuries — that's just human reality. But it's not accurate to say we have "no idea" what the original said. Scholars can trace where and when changes happened precisely because there are so many manuscripts to compare (Sightline Ministry, "The Bible: How Big a Deal is Human Error?", https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

If you want, I'm happy to dig into a specific example your uncle might raise (like a particular "changed" verse, or the Dead Sea Scrolls comparison) — that can sometimes make this more concrete than general statistics.

That's a really fair question — and one Christians themselves have wrestled with for centuries. Let me lay out what's actually being claimed, because the key is that it's not saying God is three *and* one in the *same sense*.

**The core claim**

According to Cru's article "Understanding the Trinity," the doctrine means there is one God who eternally exists as three distinct Persons — the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It breaks down into three things held together: (1) the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons, (2) each is fully God, and (3) there is only one God ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).

**Why it's not a contradiction**

The resolution lies in a distinction between two different words: *essence* and *person*. God is one in *essence* (what he is — his being, his "substance") but three in *person* (who he is — distinct relational identities). A contradiction would only occur if Christians said God is three in the *same* way he is one — but that's not the claim. As the Spanish-language version of that same Cru article puts it, "Solo habría una contradicción si decimos que Dios es tres en la misma forma que él es uno" ("There would only be a contradiction if we said God is three in the same way he is one") — [Cru](https://www.cru.org/mx/es/crecer-y-equipar/crecimiento-espiritual/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html).

EveryStudent.com offers a simple way to picture this with math: it's not 1+1+1=3, but more like 1×1×1=1 — hence the word "Trinity" (Tri = three, Unity = one) ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)).

**Why the Bible pushes Christians to say this**

- The Father is called God (Phil. 1:2), the Son is called God (Titus 2:13), and the Holy Spirit is called God (Acts 5:3-4) — Cru points out this rules out saying they're just three names or roles for the same one thing.
- Yet they're shown as distinct: the Father sends the Son (John 3:16), the Son returns to the Father and they send the Spirit (John 14:26; Acts 2:33) — so they can't just be the same person wearing different masks ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/understanding-the-trinity.html)).
- At the same time, Scripture insists firmly there's only one God — "Höre, Israel! Der HERR ist unser Gott, der HERR allein" (Deut. 6:4) and "Ich bin der HERR, und es gibt keinen außer mir" — cited in the German EveryStudent article ([EveryStudent — German](https://www.duentscheidest.com/artikel/dreieinigkeit.html)).

**On the illustrations**

People have tried analogies — water existing as ice, liquid, and steam; or the sun giving light, heat, and radiation — but as EveryStudent notes plainly, "No illustration is going to be perfect" ([EveryStudent](https://www.everystudent.com/forum/trinity.html)). It's genuinely a mystery — one article calls it "perhaps the most mysterious, beautiful and confounding doctrine of the Christian faith" ([Cru](https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html)).

So the honest Christian answer isn't "we've fully solved this puzzle" — it's "we believe this is what Scripture reveals about God, even though it stretches our categories, because God isn't bound by the limits we are." Does that distinction between "essence" and "person" make sense, or would it help to dig into why Christians think the Bible pushes them toward this conclusion in the first place?

That's a really important question, and one that many Muslims and Christians discuss respectfully with each other. Here's how Christians typically respond, drawing on a few sources:

**Christians affirm Jesus as more than a prophet — they see him as the Son of God.** As one Cru article puts it plainly: "Muslims believe Jesus to be a prophet but not God in the flesh, whereas Christians believe that Jesus is not only a prophet but the Son of God" (Cru, [What Makes Christianity Different?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html)). A related point of difference is the crucifixion and resurrection — Muslims generally do not believe Jesus died on the cross, while for Christians, his death and resurrection are foundational truths of the faith (same source).

**On the meaning of "Son of God."** Islam strongly rejects the idea that God could have a son, seeing it as incompatible with belief in one indivisible God. Christianity, though, doesn't understand Jesus's sonship in a physical or biological sense. As EveryStudent.sk explains, Christians understand "Jesus's sonship not in a bodily sense, but in a spiritual sense. Jesus is God incarnate, who was not born of a physical union of a man and woman, but through the miraculous work of the Holy Spirit" (EveryStudent.sk, [Ježiš v islame: podobnosti a rozdiely](https://everystudent.sk/jezis-v-islame)). That source also notes that the prophet Isaiah, long before Jesus's birth, described a coming child as "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" — which Christians see as pointing forward to Jesus.

**Why Christians see Jesus as the fulfillment, not just another prophet in a line.** Islam holds that God revealed his message progressively through various prophets, with Muhammad as the last one. The Christian view, according to that same EveryStudent.sk piece, is different: "God does not change his plan. From the beginning he sent prophets to bring people back into relationship with him... Christianity does not see its faith as one stage to be replaced by another, but as the fulfillment of what God promised from the beginning" — pointing to Jesus's own words, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."

**A gentler way some Christians frame the conversation.** Rather than starting from doctrinal disagreement, some Christians choose to focus on the shared human story — that everyone is created by God, everyone has fallen short, and everyone is invited into relationship with God through what God himself did in Jesus, "God sent His Son to die for our sins, and whoever believes in Him shall have eternal life" (John 3:16, cited in Cru's [What Makes Christianity Different?](https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/what-makes-christianity-different.html)).

If you're wrestling with this question yourself — whether from a Muslim background or just curious — I'd love to hear what's drawing you to ask it. Is there a particular part of this (the crucifixion, the idea of sonship, something else) you'd like to dig into more?

That's a fair and important question — and it's worth being honest about the nuance here.

**The direct answer: Jesus never says the exact English sentence "I am God."** But there's one moment where his words in the original context carry that exact weight, without needing anyone's interpretation to get there.

**John 8:58** — Jesus says: *"Very truly I tell you, before Abraham was born, I am!"* (as quoted by Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/two-reasons-skeptics-believe-jesus-is-not-god and https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false)

That phrase "I am" isn't just a grammatical oddity — it's the same phrase God uses to name himself to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3:14 ("I AM WHO I AM"). Jesus takes that divine name and applies it to himself. The reaction of the people listening confirms they heard it that way too: according to Sightline Ministry, they immediately picked up stones to kill him for blasphemy — the punishment under Jewish law for claiming to be God (https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false).

A second strong instance, at his trial: In **Mark 14:61-63**, the high priest asks Jesus directly, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?" Jesus answers simply, **"I am."** The high priest tears his robes and cries "Blasphemy!" — again, the listeners themselves understood this as a claim to deity (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html; Sightline Ministry, https://sightlineministry.org/deity-of-christ-true-or-false).

There's also **John 10:30** — *"The Father and I are one"* — which led the Jewish leaders present to say back to him, "You, a mere man, claim to be God" (Cru, https://www.cru.org/us/en/how-to-know-god/is-jesus-god.html). That's not a later theologian's spin — that's how the people standing right there in the room reacted to his own words.

So to be candid with you: Jesus's approach was less "I hereby declare I am God" and more using language, titles, and claims (like taking God's own name, or saying "I and the Father are one") that his Jewish audience — who knew their scriptures intimately — immediately recognized as a claim to divinity. That's why I've quoted the actual sentences and also told you how the original hearers reacted, so you can weigh it yourself rather than take anyone's word for what it means.

Would you like to dig into the context of John 8:58 more, or look at how the Gospel writers themselves describe who they believed Jesus to be?

3. **Why Was Jesus Crucified?** (Cru) — discusses how Jesus' death is understood to have dealt with both sin and death itself, and to have defeated the devil's work, citing John 12:30-32 and 1 John 3:8.
   https://www.cru.org/us/en/train-and-grow/spiritual-growth/core-christian-beliefs/why-was-jesus-crucified.html

4. **Why Is the Resurrection of Jesus So Important?** (Jesus Film Project) — connects Jesus' death with His resurrection, arguing (via Paul's letters, e.g. 1 Corinthians 15) that the resurrection is what confirms the death actually accomplished forgiveness of sins.
   https://www.jesusfilm.org/blog/resurrection-important

5. **Step 1: The Christian Adventure** (Cru) — a broader overview describing Jesus' death as bridging the separation between a holy God and sinful humanity, referencing Colossians 1:13-14, 20-23.

A common thread across these: Christians generally hold that Jesus' death dealt with the guilt/penalty of sin, and that His resurrection is what confirms this was effective — it's not just his death alone but death-and-resurrection together that Christians point to.

Your uncle is raising a fair question — it's one scholars have actually studied carefully, and there's good reason to think his conclusion (that we *can't* know) is too pessimistic. Here's what the evidence shows:

**We don't have the originals, but we have a LOT of copies.** According to Sightline Ministry, "we don't have the original writings, we have many copies of these original writings which scholars call manuscripts" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-altered-over-centuries). For the New Testament specifically, there are nearly 25,000 hand-written manuscript copies of portions of it (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

**The copies overwhelmingly agree with each other.** Historians who've compared these thousands of manuscripts have concluded the New Testament we have today is "at least 99.5% accurate to the original," with the small remaining differences being things like spelling variations rather than changes in meaning (EveryStudent, same source above).

**How this compares to other ancient texts.** A helpful comparison from EveryStudent — Spanish shows that for classical works like Plato, Herodotus, or Tacitus, we typically have far fewer surviving manuscripts (5–20) and a much longer gap between the original and the earliest copy (1,000+ years) — yet historians don't doubt those texts are reliably reconstructed. The Bible has vastly more manuscript evidence and closer time gaps (https://www.cadaestudiante.com/articulos/biblia.html).

**Scholars can actually trace the changes.** Sightline Ministry notes that because there are so many manuscripts to cross-check, "scholars can identify the original reading with a high degree of confidence... scholars can clearly see the path of where and when mistakes and changes were made" (https://sightlineministry.org/bible-human-error).

**Ancient copies confirm this too.** The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls (much older Old Testament manuscripts) allowed researchers to compare them with later Bibles — they were found to be "nearly 100% identical" (EveryStudent, https://www.everystudent.com/wires/jesus-in-islam.html).

So it's not that the Bible was copied so many times that we lost track — it's more that having *so many* copies actually lets scholars cross-check and reconstruct the original text with a high degree of confidence. That said, it's a topic worth digging into more if you or your uncle are curious — there's real scholarship behind this, not just faith claims. Is there a particular part of this — like translation methods, or specific "changes" people point to — you'd like to explore further?
